subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Assalamu alaykum, and welcome to Unit 3! In this unit you are going to become a materials scientist. A materials scientist is someone who watches how things change. Today, tomorrow, and every day, the world around you is changing. The ice in your cup melts into water. The butter in the pan turns soft and runny when your mother heats it. The sugar you stir into your tea seems to vanish. These are not tricks or magic. They are science, and by the end of this unit you will be able to explain all of them yourself.

Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, experiments and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

outcomes: By the end of this unit, you will be able to do all of these things. Read them now, and read them again at the end to see how much you have grown.
Describe what happens to materials like ice, butter, and chocolate when they are heated.
Describe what happens to materials like water and melted butter when they are cooled.
Explain the words melting and freezing using your own examples.
Sort changes into two groups: changes that can be undone (reversible) and changes that cannot be undone (irreversible).
Investigate which materials dissolve in water and which do not.
Predict what will happen when you mix a material with water, and then test your idea.
Stay safe around heat and hot water while you explore.
Connect what you learn to real life in your home and community.

concepts.title: Solids, Liquids, and Gases
concepts.explanation:
Before we watch materials change, we need to know what they can change *into*. Every material around you is usually in one of three forms. Scientists call these forms the states of matter. The three states are solid, liquid, and gas. Let us meet each one.

A solid keeps its own shape. If you put a solid on the table, it just sits there and stays the same shape. Think of a date stone, a stone from the ground, a wooden spoon, or a cube of ice. You can pick a solid up and it will not run through your fingers. Solids are firm because the tiny parts inside them are holding on to each other tightly, like children in a line all holding hands and standing still.

A liquid flows. It does not keep its own shape — instead it takes the shape of whatever container you pour it into. Pour water into a round cup and it becomes round. Pour it into a tall bottle and it becomes tall. Water, camel milk, cooking oil, and tea are all liquids. In a liquid, the tiny parts are still close together, but now they can slide past each other, like children walking slowly in a crowd, gently bumping and moving around.

A gas spreads out to fill all the space it can find. Most gases are so spread out that you cannot even see them. The air all around you right now is made of gases. When water boils on the stove, some of it turns into a gas we call steam, and it floats up into the air and disappears. In a gas, the tiny parts are far apart and zooming around quickly, like children running freely all over a big open field, never holding hands at all.

Did You Know? The very same material can be a solid, a liquid, AND a gas! Water is a solid when it is ice, a liquid when you drink it, and a gas when it becomes steam. It is still water the whole time — only its state has changed.

This last fact is one of the most important ideas in the whole unit. A material can change from one state to another, but it is still the same material. Ice, water, and steam are all just water wearing different clothes. What makes it change its 'clothes'? The answer is heat. When we add heat or take heat away, materials move between solid, liquid, and gas. Let us find out how.
concepts.example: Here is a helpful way to picture it. Imagine the tiny parts inside a material are like children in a classroom. In a solid, the children are sitting very still in their places, packed close together — nobody moves, so the shape stays firm. In a liquid, the children stand up and walk slowly around the room, still close but able to slide past one another — so a liquid can flow. In a gas, the children run out into a big open field and dash around freely, far apart — so a gas spreads out everywhere. When you add heat, you give the children more energy to move, so a solid can become a liquid and a liquid can become a gas. When you take heat away, the children calm down and settle, so a gas can become a liquid and a liquid can become a solid. Hold this picture in your mind and the whole unit will make sense.

concepts.title: What Heating Does
concepts.explanation:
Heating means adding heat to make something warmer. In your home, heat comes from the sun, from a charcoal stove, from a fire, or from an oven. When you add heat to a material, the tiny parts inside it start to move faster and spread out a little. This simple idea explains so many things you see every day.

The most exciting thing heat can do is turn a solid into a liquid. We call this melting. Think about butter or ghee. When it is cool, it is a firm, yellow solid you can hold. But when your mother puts it in a warm pan to cook, it becomes soft, then shiny, then runny. The solid butter has melted into liquid butter. The heat made the tiny parts inside the butter move faster until they could slide around, and a flowing liquid is exactly what you get when the parts can slide.

You have seen melting many, many times, even if you never gave it a name. On a hot afternoon, a piece of ice left on a plate slowly turns into a puddle of water. That is melting. A bar of chocolate carried in your pocket on a warm day becomes soft and messy. That is melting. A candle burning gives a small pool of melted wax around the flame. That is melting too. Every time a solid gets hot enough and turns into a liquid, that is melting.

Here is something clever to notice: not all solids melt at the same temperature. Ice melts when it is only a little bit warm — even the warmth of your hand can melt it. Butter needs to be warmer than that before it melts. A metal spoon needs to be extremely, dangerously hot before it would melt, far hotter than anything in your kitchen. That is why we can safely stir hot food with a metal spoon — the spoon stays solid because the stove is nowhere near hot enough to melt metal.

If you keep heating a liquid, something else amazing happens. It gets so hot that it starts to bubble and turn into a gas. When water does this, we say it is boiling, and the gas it turns into is called steam. Many families boil water on a charcoal stove to make it clean and safe to drink, because boiling kills the tiny germs that can make people sick. When you watch that pot, you can see white steam rising up and floating away. The water is changing from a liquid into a gas.

Boiling water and steam are very, very hot and can burn your skin badly. Steam can burn you even when you cannot see it clearly. This is why you must always let an adult handle boiling water, and why you should never lean your face over a boiling pot. We will talk more about staying safe very soon.

Safety First: Boiling water and steam are HOT enough to burn your skin. Never touch them. Always ask an adult to handle anything on a stove or fire. For your own experiments, you will only use WARM water, never boiling water.

Heat does one more thing that is easy to miss. When many materials are heated, they get a tiny bit bigger. We call this expanding. Air expands when it is warmed. If you put a soft, half-blown balloon in the warm sun, the air inside gets warm, spreads out, and the balloon grows a little bigger. The material did not turn into a puddle, and it is still a balloon — but the warmth made it expand. This is a gentle change, but it is real, and clever builders remember it when they build roads and bridges that sit in the hot sun all day.
concepts.example: Did You Know? On very hot days, metal railway tracks and bridges expand and grow slightly longer. Builders leave small gaps in bridges so the metal has room to expand without cracking!

concepts.title: What Cooling Does
concepts.explanation:
Cooling is the opposite of heating. Cooling means taking heat away so a material becomes colder. When you take heat away, the tiny parts inside a material slow down and move closer together. If heating spreads things out, cooling brings them back in. And just as heating can turn a solid into a liquid, cooling can turn a liquid back into a solid.

When a liquid gets cold enough, it turns into a solid. We call this freezing. The clearest example is water. If you pour water into a small cup and put it in a freezer, and then come back later, the water will have turned into hard, solid ice. The liquid has frozen. The cold took heat away from the water until the tiny parts slowed right down, moved close together, and locked into a firm shape — and a firm shape is exactly what a solid is.

Freezing and melting are like two doors that lead the same way. Melting takes a solid and warms it into a liquid. Freezing takes a liquid and cools it back into a solid. If you melt an ice cube into water and then freeze that water, you get ice again. You have gone all the way there and all the way back. That is a very special kind of change, and it has its own name, which we will learn in the next big idea.
concepts.example: Melted butter or ghee does the same thing. When the pan cools down, the runny liquid butter slowly turns firm and solid again. Have you ever seen a pot of cooked food that has gone cold, with a firm pale layer on top? That layer is fat that melted while cooking and then froze solid again as the food cooled. You have been watching freezing at the dinner table your whole life.

concepts.title: Changes You Can Undo, and Changes You Cannot
concepts.explanation:
Now we come to one of the most useful ideas in all of science. Some changes can be undone, and some cannot. Learning to tell the difference will make you a very sharp scientist.

A reversible change is a change you can undo. After the change, you can get back exactly what you started with. Melting and freezing are the perfect example. If you melt ice into water, you can freeze the water and get ice again. Nothing was lost. You can go forwards (melt) and backwards (freeze) as many times as you like. Because you can reverse it — go back the way you came — we call it a reversible change.

Dissolving is usually reversible too. If you dissolve salt into water, the salt seems to disappear. But it is not gone! If you leave that salty water in a warm, sunny place, the water slowly floats away as a gas (this is called evaporation), and the salt is left behind as tiny white crystals. In fact, this is one of the oldest ways in the world to make salt: people let sea water from the Indian Ocean dry up in the sun, and the salt stays behind. The salt was hidden, not destroyed, so dissolving can be reversed.

An irreversible change is a change you CANNOT undo. Once it happens, there is no going back to what you started with. Cooking is the best example. When your family cooks an egg, the runny, clear liquid inside turns white and firm. Now try to imagine turning that cooked egg back into a raw, runny egg. You cannot do it — not by cooling it, not by any trick at all. The egg has changed forever. That is an irreversible change.

There are many irreversible changes in your kitchen and community. Baking flour and water into canjeero or bread is irreversible — you can never turn the bread back into raw batter. Burning charcoal or wood is irreversible — the wood turns into ash and smoke, and ash can never become wood again. Frying meat, roasting coffee beans, and mixing certain things together can all cause changes that cannot be undone. In an irreversible change, a brand new material is made, and the old material is gone for good.

Did You Know? When bread bakes, tiny bubbles of gas puff it up and the outside turns brown and firm. This is irreversible — no baker in the world can turn a loaf of bread back into flour and water!
concepts.example: Here is a simple way to remember the difference. Ask yourself: 'Can I get back exactly what I started with?' If the answer is yes, the change is reversible (like melting, freezing, and dissolving). If the answer is no, and a new material has been made, the change is irreversible (like cooking and burning). Melting an ice cube: reversible. Frying an egg: irreversible. With a little practice you will be able to sort them quickly.

concepts.title: When a material dissolves
concepts.explanation: When you stir sugar into a cup of tea, the sugar seems to vanish. You stir and stir, and soon you cannot see a single grain. But the sugar is not gone — taste the tea and it is sweet! The sugar has broken into pieces far too tiny to see, and those pieces have spread all through the water. This is called dissolving. The sweet, clear tea you are left with is called a solution. Materials that can dissolve, like sugar and salt, are called soluble.
concepts.example: Say this idea back in your own words: When you stir sugar into a cup of tea, the sugar seems to vanish. Then find one example of when a material dissolves around your home or outside.

explorations.title: The Great Melting Race
explorations.context: To find out where ice melts fastest: in a warm sunny place, in the cool shade, or held in your hand. Make a Guess (Hypothesis) Before you begin, write or say your guess. Which place do you think will melt the ice fastest, and why? A guess you explain is called a hypothesis. What You Need: Three ice cubes that are about the same size Three small saucers or plates A sunny spot, a shady spot, and your own warm hand Something to measure time (count slowly, or use a clock) What To Do: Put one ice cube on a saucer in a warm, sunny place. Put one ice cube on a saucer in the cool shade. Hold the third ice cube in your hand (this one melts fastest, so watch it closely). Watch all three. Notice which one turns to water first, second, and last. Record the order in the table below.
explorations.prompt: What do you predict will happen in The Great Melting Race?
explorations.answer: Carry out the great melting race, record exactly what you observe, and compare it with the prediction you wrote before you started.
explorations.hint: Predict what will happen before you start, then observe carefully. Use these words when you explain: Day 1, Day 2, Day 3.

explorations.title: From Water to Ice and Back Again
explorations.context: To watch a reversible change: turn liquid water into solid ice by freezing, then turn it back into water by melting. Make a Guess (Hypothesis) What do you think will happen to the water in the freezer? And after it freezes, do you think you can turn it back into water again? What You Need A small cup or a clean plastic container Water A freezer (ask an adult for permission) A few hours of waiting time What To Do Pour a little water into the cup. Notice that it is a liquid — it flows and takes the shape of the cup. Ask an adult to help you put the cup in the freezer. Wait several hours (leaving it overnight works well). Take the cup out. Gently touch the top. What has the water become? Now leave the cup on the table in a warm place and watch. What happens to the ice over the next hour?

explorations.title: Which Ones Dissolve?
explorations.context: To find out which everyday materials are soluble (dissolve in water) and which are insoluble (do not dissolve). Make a Guess (Hypothesis) Look at each material below and guess: will it dissolve in water, or not? Write your guesses before you test. What You Need: Four clear cups of water at room temperature A spoon of sugar, a spoon of salt, a spoon of sand, and a few drops of cooking oil A spoon for stirring Your recording sheet What To Do: Fill each cup with the same amount of water. Add sugar to the first cup and stir ten times. Watch what happens. Add salt to the second cup and stir ten times. Watch what happens. Add sand to the third cup and stir ten times. Watch what happens. Add a few drops of oil to the fourth cup and stir. Watch what happens. Record whether each material dissolved (disappeared) or did not dissolve.

explorations.title: The Fastest Way to Dissolve Sugar
explorations.context: To test whether warm water dissolves sugar faster than cold water. Make a Guess (Hypothesis) Which cup do you think will dissolve the sugar first — the warm water or the cold water? Explain your guess. What You Need One cup of cold water and one cup of warm water (warm, not hot — ask an adult) Two flat spoons of sugar (one for each cup) A spoon for stirring Something to count or measure time What To Do Put the same amount of water in each cup — one cold, one warm. Add one flat spoon of sugar to each cup at the same time. Stir each cup the same way, counting your stirs out loud. Watch closely. In which cup does the sugar disappear first? Record how long each cup took.
explorations.prompt: What do you predict will happen in The Fastest Way to Dissolve Sugar?
explorations.answer: Carry out the fastest way to dissolve sugar, record exactly what you observe, and compare it with the prediction you wrote before you started.

explorations.title: Can You Undo It?
explorations.context: To sort real changes into reversible (can be undone) and irreversible (cannot be undone). Make a Guess (Hypothesis) For each change below, guess whether you could ever get back exactly what you started with. What You Need An ice cube (melting) A little sugar and water (dissolving) A piece of paper you may fold (folding) Watch an adult toast bread or cook an egg (cooking) — observe only, do not cook yourself Your recording sheet What To Do Melt the ice cube in a warm place. Could you freeze it back into ice? (Think, or try it.) Dissolve sugar in water. Could you get the sugar back by letting the water dry away in the sun? Fold a piece of paper, then unfold it. Does the crease go away completely? Watch an adult toast bread or cook an egg. Could you ever turn it back into raw bread or a raw egg? Decide for each one: reversible or irreversible? Record your answers.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 1
workedExamples.prompt: When a solid gets hot and turns into a liquid, this is called: A) freezing B) melting C) dissolving D) mixing
workedExamples.solution: 1 B — melting A solid turning into a liquid when heated is called melting.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 2
workedExamples.prompt: When a liquid gets cold and turns into a solid, this is called: A) melting B) boiling C) freezing D) dissolving
workedExamples.solution: 2 C — freezing A liquid turning into a solid when cooled is called freezing.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 3
workedExamples.prompt: Which of these is a liquid? A) ice B) a stone C) camel milk D) a wooden spoon
workedExamples.solution: 3 C — camel milk Milk flows and takes the shape of its cup, so it is a liquid.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 4
workedExamples.prompt: Which of these is a solid? A) water B) a block of ice C) steam D) cooking oil
workedExamples.solution: 4 B — a block of ice Ice keeps its own shape and is firm, so it is a solid.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 5
workedExamples.prompt: When you boil water, it turns into a gas called: A) smoke B) steam C) fog D) ice
workedExamples.solution: 5 B — steam Boiling water turns into a gas called steam.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 6
workedExamples.prompt: Which material will dissolve in water? A) sand B) sugar C) a small stone D) cooking oil
workedExamples.solution: 6 B — sugar Sugar is soluble — it dissolves and disappears into water.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 7
workedExamples.prompt: Which material will not dissolve in water? A) salt B) sugar C) sand D) coffee
workedExamples.solution: 7 C — sand Sand is insoluble — it sinks and does not dissolve.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 8
workedExamples.prompt: A change you can undo, like melting ice, is called: A) reversible B) irreversible C) permanent D) soluble
workedExamples.solution: 8 A — reversible A change you can undo, like melting ice, is reversible.

rules.title: Heating Expands, Cooling Contracts
rules.text: Remember how heat makes materials expand and grow a little bigger? Cooling does the opposite. When materials cool down, they usually get a tiny bit smaller. We call this contracting. Take that balloon that grew bigger in the warm sun and move it into a cool, shady place. As the air inside cools down and pulls together, the balloon shrinks a little and becomes softer. The balloon did not break or change into anything else — the cool air simply made it contract.

rules.title: Melting, Freezing and Boiling
rules.text: Heating: parts move faster and spread out. Solids can melt; liquids can boil. Cooling: parts slow down and pull together. Liquids can freeze. Melting and freezing are opposites. Boiling and cooling steam are opposites too.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What are the three states of matter? Give one example of each.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 1. The three states are solid (example: ice), liquid (example: water or camel milk), and gas (example: air or steam). Each state behaves in its own way.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain what melting means and give one example from your home.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 2. Melting is when a solid turns into a liquid because it gets hot. Example: butter or ghee melting in a warm pan.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain what freezing means and give one example from your home.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 3. Freezing is when a liquid turns into a solid because it gets cold. Example: water turning into ice in a freezer.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What is the difference between a reversible change and an irreversible change?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 4. A reversible change can be undone so you get back what you started with (like melting and freezing). An irreversible change cannot be undone and makes a new material (like cooking an egg).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What does it mean when we say sugar is soluble?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 5. Soluble means the material CAN dissolve. Sugar is soluble because it disappears into water and makes a solution.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What does it mean when we say sand is insoluble?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 6. Insoluble means the material CANNOT dissolve. Sand is insoluble because it stays as sand and sinks to the bottom.

I can describe what happens to materials like ice, butter, and chocolate when they are heated.
I can describe what happens to materials like water and melted butter when they are cooled.
I can explain the words melting and freezing using your own examples.
I can sort changes into two groups: changes that can be undone (reversible) and changes that cannot be undone (irreversible).
I can investigate which materials dissolve in water and which do not.
I can predict what will happen when you mix a material with water, and then test your idea.
I can stay safe around heat and hot water while you explore.
